title: Lachlan Denton - Breaking and Entering
summary: Lauran and simon talks to Lachlan about his new album and his brother who has passed away and the his brother was in.
transcript:
Lachlan Denton joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studio for this Breaking and Entering interview, dated 11 June 2019, to discuss his forthcoming album A Brother and the music he shared with his late brother, Zac Denton. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: It's nice to have you back. We're speaking on the eve of your leaving for Germany, after some significant shows. Late last month you played Spunk Records' twentieth anniversary at the Sydney Opera House, marked as your final show with The Ocean Party. What was that evening like for you?

Lachlan: It was strange. We played a bunch of shows over the last couple of months that were our final shows. The Opera House was really nice, and everything was surreal about it. I thought it was going to have this massive weight once it finished, but it just happened. It was so unlike every other show I've played in my time playing music that it was a different experience. I thought it would feel like a final show, but it felt like something totally different entirely. It was nice.

Simon: A lovely opportunity to perform alongside labelmates. Spunk Records is a family as much as a record label.

Lachlan: Absolutely. It was nice for Aaron Curnow, who runs the label, who's an absolute gentleman. It was nice to see him be able to have that. It was really lovely.

Lauren: The band may no longer be writing or performing together, but it lives on in the records and listeners' lives. What's been The Ocean Party's place in your life, and what are some of your strongest memories?

Lachlan: The biggest part of The Ocean Party was always the friendship. Every member of that band is still one of my best friends. To have spent pretty much my whole twenties travelling in beat-up vans, sleeping on floors and in the van, is priceless. I'm about to turn thirty. Especially having lost Zac, I drove back from Wagga today with my mum and was speaking to her about having such a tangible thing, to have had that with my brother, spent that time and have those records. It's all the friendship and relationships. I know it doesn't have to be tangible to be important, but it's nice to look back and have those records and memories of those tours.

Simon: You and Zac were brothers, bandmates and friends, working together for years. Did you always know you'd be in a band together?

Lachlan: Not at all, actually. I'm about six years older than Zac, so through high school it was enough of an age gap. The closest we got when we were younger was that I tried to make him skateboard. I grew up in a tiny town called Tarcutta, which has three hundred people, so I had no friends, really. I tried to shape him into the friend I wanted. But by high school I'd moved away and met my close friends who became my bandmates. I remember coming back to Wagga at a certain point and realising my little brother had become this fully formed, not an adult, but a young adult. He was playing music himself, a capable musician, and such a soft, gentle person, a great person to be around. At that point I knew I wanted to play music with him, spend more time with him and become closer.

Simon: You and Zac worked closely and both wrote quickly and extensively. What beliefs or practices did you share about music and its place in your lives?

Lachlan: We're both kind of flippant. Both Zac and I, and for the most part the other members of The Ocean Party, have always had that philosophy. I've always seen music as a kind of time capsule, a picture of it over time, and I think he was very much like that as well. So much in music is taken up by things outside the creative aspect. You can spend a week or a month making a record, then some artists spend a year or two getting it ready for release and putting it out. We were far more interested in the creative side of making music. I wasn't content, and Zac was never content, to make a record and do promotion for two years. We just wanted to move on to the next thing and keep making music, whether it was making an impact or not.

Lauren: What did Zac particularly teach you about songwriting?

Lachlan: I always said to Zac that I was jealous of him coming to music in the way he did. He moved to Melbourne when he was eighteen. When I was eighteen I was still living in Wagga, figuring it out. I think I was still imitating at his age. It's easy when you're young, because you're constantly listening to music made by adults, to fall into the trap of pretending you're an adult when you're not. I said to him early on, don't be afraid to explore your naivety and talk about those things. The most important thing about music is exploring whatever you want to explore. If you spend that time just imitating, I don't know if you get as much out of it. Through that, I feel like I got to watch him grow up as a songwriter. There were things he wouldn't say to us but would happily put in a song. That's incredibly important. I think he very much taught me that. I gave him a push in a certain direction, then I was lucky enough to have that come back and learn from him.

Lachlan: Not long after Zac passed away, I almost didn't like it, but I knew that I would probably end up writing music about it, because that's inevitably what I've always done. But it's conflicting because it's grief. As much as you don't want to admit it, music is a commercial venture. Not to say I've ever made money from music, but it is a commercial venture. It sounds cheesy, but I don't think I totally had a say in it. When I sat down to play guitar for probably the first time after Zac passed away, there wasn't going to be anything else I could sing about. That was what I was going to do. All my songs, at least for probably the last five years, have been like a mantra. I don't know if that's the right word. I'm not someone to sit down and write about how everything's awful and wallow in that. I try to use songwriting to explore those things and hopefully come out the other side in a positive light. When I started writing about what happened, I was thinking about what I could take from it in a positive way. Just before Zac passed away, I'd been listening to an interview with Leigh Sales. I don't know if she'd just written a book called Any Ordinary Day, about grief. In the interview she was talking about the positives that come out of these situations. It's not something you think about often, but I loved Zac very much and don't want to see only negatives come out of him passing away, because that seems an awful waste. When I started writing, I had that in mind: how can I pull this apart and think about how lucky I was to have that time with him, and how much it's taught me about the community I exist in? It's a cliché, but people really come together. The way friends are there in these situations is life-affirming, and you need those things in those times. I wanted to write music that was life-affirming. It was sad to write, but hopefully it's not indulgent sadness.

Lauren: Not at all. It's a celebration of Zac's life and a reflection of the community.

Simon: You've assembled that community around you in Studio Magic. Could we talk about this band, and how making the record reflects those connections?

Lachlan: Zac recorded a lot of music while he was with us, and he was always pushing people. Our community has always pushed friends to write music. I've always offered to record friends. When I wrote these songs, I wanted to come at it from a similar angle. On the last record I made, I played everything, but this time I wanted everyone to be totally involved. Anila, my partner, who'd never played music before, plays on the record. My friend Rose, who'd never played in a band before, plays guitar. My friend Dain, who I've been friends with for ages, has played in plenty of bands, but I just wanted to play music with him. Ambrin, Anila's sister and a great friend of mine, played in Pregnancy with Zac. They were living together, and he pushed her to play music. I wanted not just friends involved, but people who hadn't played music before.

Lauren: The album concludes with a Hobby Farm song, one of your brother's many bands. What's the personal significance of that song?

Lachlan: I was changing Zac's rego from his name to mine. When he passed away, everything had to be sorted with his belongings, and my parents wanted me to take his car. I had to go through all those totally unromantic, awful things. I was walking back from VicRoads in Carlton to get the tram home, and I put that record on. It's a song Zac wrote to my nan. He was unashamedly her favourite. She was very vocal about him being her favourite grandson, and he spent a lot of time on my grandparents' farm growing up. She played favourites, for sure. In that song he's telling her not to cry, he'll be all right. It was the first time I'd listened to it since he passed away. Having him sing that back to me was really affecting. Making the record, I knew I wanted to put one of Zac's songs on it. It's important to me to make sure any music he made that hasn't come out gets released. I've been slowly working through that, and some of the little-heard stuff, like the Hobby Farm record I put out. No one probably knows that record, and it's amazing. It's called Braeside. He made it when he was about twenty. The instrumentation, which he did all himself, is stunning, and the lyrics still have that naivety I love. It was a song that affected me, and another way to hopefully have people hear it and go and listen to more of Zac's music.

Lachlan: He had a very bizarre way of phrasing his lyrics. When he used to write songs, he'd come in with this big old diary, an out-of-date A4 diary or some strange book. He'd have a page full of lyrics he'd poured out, then go through and sing it to the song he'd written. I'm not sure he ever wrote lyrics to songs. He'd have the most insane phrasing. Amanda was telling me about trying to sing backing vocals to this total chaos of phrasing. Sometimes he'd get to the end of a line and just end it there.

Simon: The lack of editing is what's special about listening to so much of Zac's music. It's a mix of folk storytelling and beautiful imagery, which I don't think you'd get if you were pulling the songs down.

Lachlan: It has this surreal realism, fragments of his life, from a large picture of a farm down to a tiny phrase or image. It's so inspiring.

Lachlan: He was very close with my grandparents, so he has so many songs about their farm and spending time there. The song 'Nothing Grows' is about my grandparents. It's uncomfortably autobiographical, which is beautiful for us, but also hard to hear.

Simon: The Ocean Party, your music and Zac's music are sincere and vulnerable, encouraging us as listeners to share more of ourselves. I think an important message from your album is to appreciate and be grateful for those moments and connections.

Lachlan: Absolutely. If there's anything I'd want people to take from the record, it's that, to be thankful. I don't want to push a message down people's throats that they need to suddenly tell everyone they love them every day. We can appreciate these things in hindsight, and we still have those memories, which is incredibly powerful.

Lauren: Thank you for being so open with us and sharing these beautiful memories of Zac.

Lachlan: Thanks so much for having me.
